claims.text: Conventionally synthesized refractory HEAs generally have a relatively coarse, undeveloped microstructure with limited nanoscale precipitate control.
Multi-pass thermo-mechanical deformation followed by aging at approximately 1000 °C for approximately 5 hours will produce fine nanoscale B2 precipitates.
The B2 precipitates produced by the proposed treatment will be coherent.
The proposed deformation and aging treatment will refine the grain-boundary network.
The fine coherent precipitates will act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The engineered precipitate and grain-boundary structure will provide abundant sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
The treatment will increase elevated-temperature yield strength relative to an untreated RHEA.
The treatment will improve elevated-temperature ductility relative to an untreated RHEA.
The treated alloy will retain resistance to thermal degradation during service at 800–1200 °C.
The treated alloy will have irradiation-induced defect accumulation similar to or lower than the untreated baseline under heavy-ion irradiation or helium implantation.
The treatment will mitigate radiation-damage accumulation without causing unstable intermetallic-phase evolution.
Significant departures from the proposed aging temperature or duration may produce undesirable coarse intermetallic phases.
Long thermal exposures can coarsen BCC and B2 phases and generate potentially detrimental intermetallic precipitation in a refractory high-entropy superalloy.
BCC refractory HEAs can exhibit irradiation tolerance associated with lattice distortion and chemical complexity.
W-Ta-Cr-V refractory HEAs have shown suppressed dislocation-loop formation, smaller helium bubbles, and no radiation-induced grain-boundary segregation under ion irradiation or helium implantation.
Untreated refractory HEAs typically have less optimal mechanical performance and a less controllable microstructure under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits irradiation resistance similar to the baseline, whereas the falsification rule treats equivalent irradiation-induced damage as falsifying. An equivalent-damage result is therefore simultaneously predicted and defined as failure.

The baseline is described as differing by omission of post-deformation aging, but the experimental baseline uses only the standard synthesis route while the treated arm adds both multi-pass forging and aging. This prevents the experiment from attributing an observed effect specifically to the post-deformation aging treatment.
